newsitem.title: UK: Will Channel 5 make UK's commercial TV pie bigger?.
newsitem.headline: Will Channel 5 make UK's commercial TV pie bigger?.

text.p: As Britain's fifth terrestrial television network counts down to its March launch, it predicts half its audience will come from the state-run BBC television stations, giving it clout with advertisers eager to reach a wider audience.

But others are skeptical that Channel 5 will lure many viewers from Britain's two, non-commercial stations. They believe it will draw largely from Channel 4 -- the state-owned commercial network designed to offer alternative programming to the mass market-oriented commercial ITV network.

What can be agreed is that the scheduled launch of Channel 5 on March 30 will add a significant new element to Britain's television landscape. The 24-hour-a-day network -- a joint venture of British media groups Pearson Plc and United News & Media Plc, U.S. investment firm Warburg Pincus and Luxembourg broadcast group CLT -- will add 61,000 minutes a year of commercial airtime, based on the seven minutes of advertising it can sell per hour.
Channel 5 insists the additional commercial time is a commodity that advertisers have been clamouring for.

"I think the greatest frustration for a number of advertisers has been that half of all television viewing is not available to them for advertising," Nick Milligan, director of sales for Channel 5, told Reuters in an interview. "So advertisers have been screaming for more minutage, either for more minutes on the existing ITV and Channel 4 (networks) or that the BBC be allowed to carry advertising."

Although cable and satellite television is available to advertisers, Milligan said its relatively small penetration to roughly 20 percent of British households greatly restricts its attractiveness to advertisers.

Milligan, meanwhile, said Channel 5 expects to win about six percent of Britain's total television audience when it comes to air in March. "We hope at least half of that will come from the non-commercial sector, in other words the BBC channels," he said.
The six percent share of the total TV market would translate into a 10 percent market share of the UK's commercial television audience.
Outsiders have estimated Channel 5 could win from three to eight percent of the TV market, said Steve Hyde broadcast director for Zenith Media, a media buyer and planner owned by Cordiant Plc.

"History tells us that when new things launch, it's channels with the smallest franchises that people move away from," said Hyde. "If that were to replicate itself, Channel 4 is likely to suffer more than ITV."

Martin Bowley, managing director of Carlton Sales, the commercial sales arm for ITV licensee Carlton Communications Plc, said that while ITV is sure to lose some audience and advertisers to Channel 5, Channel 4 is most vulnerable. "They seem to be attacking Channel 4 aggressively at the moment," Bowley told Reuters.
The key factor these days to advertisers is the individual programmes. "Our advertisers are focusing much more on what individual programmes will deliver their campaign," Bowley said.

Channel 5, which is aiming for an audience aged 16 to 49 that will fit between the profile audiences for Channel 4 and cable and satellite, expects to lure advertisers in its early days with lower rates, Milligan said.
Channel 4 offered ad rates about 10 percent below ITV when it became an independent network in 1993.
Milligan declined to forecast how long it will take Channel 5 to compete equally with ITV on rates.
As well as drawing advertisers which already have a presence on ITV and Channel 4, Milligan said the network will seek new television advertisers.

"We'll be giving commercial incentives for new advertisers to use TV again," he said. Channel 5 may offer to provide commercial production to new advertisers, as well as offering introductory ad rates, he said.
"Because we're a mass audience, every advertiser I've spoken to would wish to use the channel," depending on ad rates, Milligan said.

Zenith's Hyde, meanwhile, said advertisers are playing more of a wait-and-see game with Channel 5, waiting to see if its programmes can deliver the kind of audiences they want before committing advertising spending.

Where Channel 5 may win, however, is in programme sponsorship, Hyde said. Many advertisers interested in sponsorship deals who may be put off by the high cost of entering into such deals with ITV, may find a home with a new channel eager to win sponsors at a sharply lower cost, he said.
